tagline.text: A current-swept advanced drift site at the tip of the Calumpan Peninsula

location.label: Location
location.text: Waters off Cazador Point, southern tip of the Calumpan Peninsula, Mabini

children.text: Mainit Corner is a dive site at the southern tip of the Calumpan Peninsula in Mabini, Batangas, off the point the charts call Cazador Point. Unusually for Anilao, it is swept by strong currents, which suits experienced divers hoping for big gorgonian walls and schooling fish.

Mainit Corner is one of the southernmost sites on the Anilao dive map. It lies at the tip of the Calumpan Peninsula, in the narrow strait where Batangas Bay begins, and its official geographic name is Cazador Point. "Mainit" means "hot" in Tagalog, and divers came to call the site Mainit because of a small hot spring on the shore. More than one well-known site in Anilao carries the Mainit name, so be sure to confirm exactly which one you are booking.

Unlike the rest of Anilao, famed as a paradise of tiny creatures, this site is about the scenery that moving water creates. Several times a day the tides push through the narrow strait and sweep the underwater terrain, so it is good for wide-angle shots among the rock mounds, and fish schools become lively when the water is running. One dive resort bills the site as Anilao's "High-Voltage Fish Highway." The same current is why it is rated as not suitable for beginners.

Depth figures differ by source. One dive resort lists 5–60 m and says the apex slopes gradually to about 40 m before dropping steeply past 70 m, while another guide gives 5–35 m. Recreational divers usually stay above the drop-off, so the depths they actually use are much shallower. Either way, this is a site for divers who stick to their planned depth and time.

Some reports say that in the shallows you can start relatively calmly with the boat anchored near the rock that breaks the surface (the bommie). On the sheltered side you can find nudibranchs and small crustaceans, so some Anilao-style macro diving is possible too. This guide assumes a big difference between strong-current days and calm days, and sets out how to plan and what to watch for.

blocks.title: The hot spring point on Cazador Point

children.text: A small hot spring on the shore gave the site its name. The official name is Cazador Point, and divers call it Mainit. It is where the peninsula's tip turns toward Batangas Bay.

blocks.title: Three rock mounds at the apex

children.text: Three large rock mounds are said to sit at about

near the tip of the apex. The water is broken up behind the mounds, which makes a good place to rest, and wrasses, sweetlips, anthias and groupers gather around them. Oriental sweetlips are often seen hiding in the shadows of the rocks.

blocks.title: Soft corals and sea fan walls

children.text: Dense soft corals color the deep slopes, while sea fans, sponges and whip corals grow on the shallower walls. The shallows on the east side have soft corals while the west side has almost none, a clear contrast.
You can drift along the coral walls on the current. Some say the fish are at their richest when the water is running, and the usual approach is for a guide to follow along with the boat.

In the current you may meet schools of silvery chevron barracuda, and trevallies and tuna have also been reported. Blacktip sharks are seen occasionally but are becoming rarer, and sea turtles sometimes pass by. Sources add that fish numbers are lower than before because of overfishing.
Around the rock that breaks the surface, the dive starts at about
8 m
and continues along a gentle wall. One diver's report from this area lists pink nudibranchs, lionfish, juvenile sweetlips, a tiny white anglerfish and even a pygmy seahorse.
The site is described as lying within the Mabini-Tingloy Protected Landscape and Seascape. Do not drop anchors on the coral or touch marine life, and follow local environmental fees and rules.

blocks.title: Telling it apart from Mainit Bubbles

children.text: A separate site on the same peninsula, known as Mainit Bubbles, has hot bubbles rising from the seabed. In 2021 local media reported that the bubbles increased around the time of the Taal Volcano eruption, and a geology agency said they were not dangerous. The names are similar, so always check which site you are booking.
Get a short briefing at your Anilao resort. Confirm with the guide the entry side, when the current picks up, the maximum depth and the no-fly time.

15–30 minutes
depending on where your resort is.
First dive. Start in the shallows at around
8 m
and descend slowly along the wall, following the guide's signals where the water is running.
Surface interval. On days with waves, stay close to the boat, sort out your gear and time your climb aboard.
Do the second dive only on a calm day. Look at the same site from another direction or search for macro life around the shallow bommie.
Return to the resort for lunch and log your dives. If you are flying, leave at least
18–24 hours
after your last dive.
Because Mainit is a long ride away and tied to certain current windows, a common plan is to go first thing in the morning and spend the afternoon at a nearby macro site.

Arrive at the resort, check your gear and do a check dive to settle your buoyancy and breathing.
After lunch, dive a shallow macro site. This is a step to check how you feel before doing Mainit.
Have dinner, write up your log and turn in early. Since there is a current-swept site the next day, choose a night dive only if it fits your schedule.
On the second morning, head to Mainit Corner for 1–2 dives.
After lunch, rinse your gear and check out. If you are flying out of Manila, leave plenty of time after your last dive.

items.title: From Manila by car or van

children.text: From Manila, take the SLEX and STAR Tollway through Batangas to Mabini. With normal traffic it takes about
3 hours
, but it can take longer on weekends and holidays.
Most dive resorts run a pickup van from Manila. If you have a lot of gear, the resort van is the easy choice.
Mainit Corner can only be reached by sea, so you go to an Anilao resort or dive center and board a boat.
The ride to Mainit differs by resort. One diver's report gives about 20 minutes by boat from one resort, while another resort says about 30 minutes.
Take a bus from Manila toward Batangas City, then transfer to a jeepney or tricycle bound for Mabini or Anilao. This takes a long time with luggage, so it is not recommended.
Local transport from Batangas City toward Anilao changes its schedule, so check on the spot.
You cannot walk to Mainit Corner; you reach it by bangka. The resort or dive center arranges it to fit your schedule.
The Anilao pier charges environmental and terminal fees separately. Amounts can change, so confirm when you book.

Some sources say Mainit can be dived year-round, but one guide recommends the calm November–May dry season. Its position at the tip of the peninsula means that whichever way the wind blows, one side is sheltered, which is a feature of this site.

During the Habagat (southwest monsoon, roughly June–October) entry is said to be from the east, the Batangas Bay side, and during the Amihan (northeast monsoon, roughly November–March) it is reversed to the west. Matching the tide window matters most, so follow your guide's judgment.

To reach Mainit Corner you take a boat from an Anilao resort. Long-running dive resorts line the coast of the Calumpan Peninsula in Mabini, and the ride to the site depends on where your resort is. When booking, ask first whether the resort includes current sites like Mainit in its schedule.

Meals are mostly taken at the resort. Meal times are set around the dive schedule, so let them know in advance if you need a special diet. Local eateries around the peninsula are worth a stop after a short boat transfer, but check their hours on the spot.
Because this is a current-swept site, ask first how the guide and boat operate, and go with a reliable resort and guide.
Bring a bright surface buoy, a whistle and a surface marker so you can be seen from the boat.
If you shoot underwater, bring a wide-angle lens. Behind the rock mounds the current is weaker, which makes it a good place to take photos.
Water temperature is usually 26–30℃, but a thermocline can make it suddenly colder. A hood or a thin suit is a good idea.
Visibility is usually in the 10–30 m range. It varies with weather and tide, so check conditions on the morning of the dive.
As a general rule, leave at least 18–24 hours after your last dive before flying.
Beginners should build experience first at gentler sites such as Twin Rocks and Cathedral Rock instead of Mainit.

This is an advanced site with down-currents and strong currents. If you are caught in a down-current, you are advised not to cling to the wall or fight it, but to swim away from the reef into open water.
Below the apex the bottom drops steeply past 70 m, so watch your depth gauge to avoid exceeding recreational limits.
On days with waves, entering and exiting can be difficult, so time your climb back onto the boat with the waves.
One report describes about 12 boats crowded nearby on a fine day, with anchors dragging and boats bumping. At the surface, watch for boat noise and positions.
Information gets mixed up with Mainit Bubbles and Mainit Point of the same name, so reconfirm with your guide which site it is, the entry direction and the depth.
Sea conditions, rules and environmental fees change often, so check the latest notices before you leave.
The Mabini dive area where Mainit Corner lies, with about 40 sites. It is famous for macro diving and blackwater diving.
A beach on Tingloy Island that is good for snorkeling on a rest day. You have to get there by boat.
A current-swept dive area about
1.5–2 hours
by boat from Anilao. Recommended for advanced and above divers.
